nit: this is just preference but i don't like having `std::exit` all over the code.

It messes with the symmetry of constructor/destructor, as some destructors will not be called.

https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/utility/program/exit

My preference would be to pass some return value in error case and then `std::exit` in on place, or not `std::exit` at all and just return from main function.

std::exit and std::cerr were put in as extending the previous logic in this function. I'm fine with moving logs over to lg2.

That said, if we have critical system resources that aren't being cleaned up by the OS on process exit, destructors won't save us in general and we likely have a design flaw. std::exit isn't the only way that this program can end without firing destructors.

From a code design perspective, yes, returning from main is cleaner; from a "are resources cleaned up" perspective, if we're relying on destructors firing on process exit paths, things are kind of broken.

> std::exit and std::cerr were put in as extending the previous logic in this function. I'm fine with moving logs over to lg2.

Yes, usually implementing similar to the existing code is a good idea.

But the existing code here is not amazing so we may want to go a different route.

### lg2

For the lg2, you can just also pick and choose from https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/entity-manager/+/83682 for whichever files/functions you consider in scope of your change (or just convert the entire file in a patch before/after this one).

### local reasoning and `std::exit`

regular functions usually return or throw something.

If we `std::exit` anywhere along the way then local reasoning is broken, because

in function `a` we now need to consider the `std::exit` that happens in function `c` along the caller relationship `a -> b -> c`

because any code after the call to `b` will not be run.

And if local reasoning is broken, the code will become unmaintainable (IMO).

### funny example of how EM uses destructors

> From a code design perspective, yes, returning from main is cleaner; from a "are resources cleaned up" perspective, if we're relying on destructors firing on process exit paths, things are kind of broken.

https://github.com/openbmc/entity-manager/blob/fd939286bad96a52004925893ae5b98d6b67a623/src/entity_manager/perform_scan.cpp#L603
this is `scan::PerformScan::~PerformScan()`.

It's a destructor which either makes a shared_ptr (of another instance of itself) or calls a callback.

### program portability and `std::exit`

programs using `std::exit` are hard to turn into libraries. Since control flow does not go back through the main function.

### unit testing and `std::exit`

It's hard to test code using `std::exit` because the test will ... exit.

So it's not possible to do any assertions after such an exit has taken place.

Also not possible to run multiple tests in sequence in the same process.

we haven't changed any of the operating assumptions of this function, namely that if the config is malformed enough, we refuse to parse it, and if we don't have a proper config, we can't do anything well enough to move on with the process. Which, for config parsing, is generally a decent assumption IMO, separate from concerns about function design or which entity in the callgraph makes that decision.

I understand your points about unit testing and local reasoning, and I generally agree with them. In its current form this function isn't unit testable in any way. Its hidden in a .cpp file, and relies on global variables as is.

I don't see any of the code in this entire file as being a decent target for a separable library, there are much bigger fish to fry around that, i.e. that dbus logic is deeply intertwined with business logic.

This is a function that runs at startup, once, by design. If this was deep into a dbus driven callgraph, I would absolutely agree with you that this needs to be fixed.

If we want to refactor this function and make it unit testable, etc, its a decent target for that IMO. That should be a separate commit from a feature add, however.

You can easily reduce the number of `std::exit` being added here by extracting your address block list parsing code into a separate function like `loadAddressBlockList`.

Then just `std::exit` once in `loadBlocklist`. in case `loadAddressBlockList` fails.

As of this patchset, the function very long anyways.

I would say I'm not a huge fan of having std::exit all over the code either, but I don't want to hold up this review for something that this method already does, and follows the existing standard.

Absolutely I would entertain patches that cleaned this up and refactored it, but as is, this is the "correct" way to handle errors in this function.

> for something that this method already does, and follows the existing standard.

Agree on this point, we do not need to introduce an inconsistency into the existing function.

This feature should go into a separate function since with this patch the function is around 139 lines.

https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines#Rf-single
https://github.com/openbmc/docs/blob/master/style/cpp/tidy-desired.md

I do not see any reason why that would be difficult. The code for this feature is at the end of the function. Just take whatever is needed as reference parameter and then call the new function at the end of `loadBlocklist`

Its certainly possible, but would be a relatively large refactor of the code base, which I'm not opposed to but I don't want to tie that refactor to this change. There's a number of places where having an object (or more) would make some of this easier, especially around passing around the contents of the FRU and this kind of bus level metadata. Specifically on rescanOneBus and its ilk, I don't think a FruDevice should be responsible for that (rescanOneBus & rescanBusses should probably return constructed FruDevices), but thats the kind of bikeshedding we can do in a different review.
